name: Prize crossword No 23,334
preamble: Most across solutions are of a kind and most of their clues lack definition. This puzzle was published in the print version of The Guardian under the title "A walk on the wild side".

clue.text: Doctor, thematically American

blocks.note: first meaning: an informal word for a physician
second meaning: the American spelling of medick, a clover-like wild plant, so it fits the puzzle's theme

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says the across answers are wild flowers. The plant is spelt medick in Britain and medic in America, hence 'thematically American'.
explanation.definitionFit: A medic is a colloquial name for a physician or army medical orderly, and in American usage also names the plant medick.

clue.text: Get all you can from lawyers in café

blocks.note: to milk something is to exploit it to the full
the Bar is the body of barristers

explanation.surface: Advice to fleece the lawyers you meet over coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests exploiting lawyers sitting in a café; in fact the café is the definition and the two halves stand side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A milk bar is a simple snack shop selling milk drinks and light meals, a kind of informal eating place.

clue.text: Duck, short form, without its head or tail

indicators.note: losing either end is allowed, and the word has the same letter at both ends, so either cut works

blocks.note: Disney's famous cartoon duck

explanation.surface: A note on abbreviating a duck's name by trimming its ends.
explanation.walkthrough: DONALD begins and ends with D, so dropping the tail leaves DONAL; 'head or tail' is a sly hint that either D could go.
explanation.definitionFit: Donal is the Irish form of the name Donald, a shortened version lacking the final letter.

clue.text: Airless round cathedral?

blocks.note: first meaning: stuffy, muggy weather
second meaning: the enclosed precinct surrounding a cathedral

explanation.surface: A stuffy day around a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: The two parts look like one description of the weather around a cathedral, but each is a separate meaning of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Close weather is humid and oppressive, and a cathedral close is the walled grounds and houses around the building.

clue.text: The girl in the rainbow

blocks.note: first meaning: a common girl's name
second meaning: the colour at the inner edge of the spectrum

explanation.surface: A girl standing in a rainbow, as in a children's story.
explanation.walkthrough: As the preamble warns, the flower meaning is left out; the clue gives a name and a colour instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Violet is both a traditional female forename and the last of the seven named spectrum colours, after indigo.

clue.text: Bigwig and bigger one has 45 beheaded

blocks.note: a very important person
the comparative ending that turns big into bigger

explanation.surface: A boast about important people and an even bigger one decapitating someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 45 across is MADDER; beheaded it is ADDER. The viper is the larger group of snakes to which the adder belongs, so it 'has' one.
explanation.definitionFit: Vipers are a family of venomous snakes, and the common European adder is one of its members.

clue.text: Skip people who deserve it

blocks.note: the Order of Merit, an honour for those of great merit
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suggestion to pass over those who have earned something.
explanation.walkthrough: OM stands for the Order of Merit, a British honour; its members are literally people who deserve it.
explanation.definitionFit: To skip something is to leave it out or pass over it, a straightforward synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Student in French n-number

blocks.note: élève is French for pupil
the letter written before the hyphen

explanation.surface: A stammering French student trying to say a number.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter 'n-number' looks like a typo, but it supplies the final letter, leaving 'number' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is a cardinal figure, the integer following ten, so it is a straightforward example of a number.

clue.text: Second help after termination of disease, one hears

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it, so the order of the parts is set by this word

blocks.note: the suffix ending many names of inflammatory diseases
standard abbreviation for second
aid means help

explanation.surface: Seeking further help once an illness has run its course, so the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Termination' means the word ending -itis, as in tonsillitis, not the end of an illness. This is one of the across clues that is not a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases introduce hearsay: something reported by others rather than known at first hand.

clue.text: 36 for Lolita?

blocks.note: surface reading: 36 down is EATS, so something to eat, a small pastry
setter's reading: Nabokov's Lolita is a young temptress, a little tart in slang

explanation.walkthrough: A tartlet is a small pastry, so it counts as 36 down, EATS; tart is also slang for a loose woman, and Lolita is a very young one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a small pastry case with filling, and jokingly suggests a juvenile version of the slang sense.

clue.text: Reporter's abandoned Christmas's lists

indicators.note: a reporter passes on what is said, so we use the spoken version of the words

blocks.note: shed means abandoned and Yule is Christmas

explanation.surface: A journalist has given up on writing Christmas lists.
explanation.walkthrough: This relies on the British pronunciation with a soft 'sh' start rather than the American 'sk'.
explanation.definitionFit: Schedules are timetables or itemised plans, so they are tabulated records of items, which is what lists are.

clue.text: Fishy dwellings, as in song

indicators.note: one thing set inside another, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: an aria is an operatic solo
qua is Latin for 'in the capacity of', i.e. as

explanation.surface: Homes for fish, as described in some song.
explanation.walkthrough: Qua, Latin for 'in the capacity of', is the crossword's usual way to render 'as'; it goes after the opening letter of the operatic solo.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquaria are glass tanks where fish are kept, so in a playful sense they are fish homes.

clue.text: Old and feeble stranger starts dying outside

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept
to be outside is to surround, so these letters wrap round the other piece

blocks.note: the opening pair of letters of this word
stranger means more odd

explanation.surface: An elderly, frail stranger beginning to die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' is plural, so take the first two letters of 'dying'; those two then go either side of the comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: Doddery describes someone shaky and tottering from age, so infirm and elderly.

clue.text: I leave lion to fellow lions

indicators.note: when one letter leaves a word it simply drops out

blocks.note: the big cat with its I removed
a don is a college fellow
a pride is a group of lions

explanation.surface: Someone bequeathing a lion to the other lions.
explanation.walkthrough: London pride is a saxifrage with pink starry flowers; a fellow of an Oxbridge college is a don.
explanation.definitionFit: London pride is a low-growing saxifrage with rosettes and pink blooms, one of the wild plants of the theme.

clue.text: What Santa says about  ... about German adder

indicators.note: to be about something is to be round it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: Father Christmas's traditional laugh
re means about or concerning
und is German for 'and', the word that adds one thing to another

explanation.surface: Santa chatting about a German snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adder' is not the snake: it is something that adds, the conjunction 'and', here in German. Horehound is a hairy wild herb of the mint family.
explanation.definitionFit: Horehound is a downy grey-leaved herb, used in old cough remedies, and one of the wild plants of the theme.

clue.text: Let high finance's lost leader put debtor inside

indicators.note: a word that has lost its leader is missing its opening letter
putting pieces down one after another builds the word in sequence
placing something inside means it goes within the other letters

blocks.note: H marks high pressure on a weather map
the money word minus its first letter
DR is the bookkeeping abbreviation for debtor

explanation.surface: An instruction to let top-level money men lock up whoever owes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let' looks like a verb meaning allow, but it is the noun from tennis and law, as in 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: A let is an obstruction or impediment, an old sense surviving in the legal phrase 'without let or hindrance'.

clue.text: William's fruit?

blocks.note: surface reading: a man named William owns some fruit
setter's reading: William is Bill, and the fruit is a berry belonging to him

explanation.walkthrough: Bill is the usual short form of William, and 'Bill's berry' sounds just like the dark-blue moorland fruit, spelt with one L.
explanation.definitionFit: The bilberry, or whortleberry, is a low wild shrub of heaths whose small blue-black berries are eaten.

clue.text: Be sensitive about names

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: to feel is to be sensitive
n is an abbreviation for name, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Advice to be careful how you talk about names.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no definition: the preamble says the across clues mostly give only wordplay, and the answer is a wild flower. Fennel is a tall yellow-flowered umbellifer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fennel is a tall aniseed-scented plant with feathery leaves and yellow umbels, growing wild on coasts and waste ground.

clue.text: Note in terrible sad song

indicators.note: something placed in something else sits inside it

blocks.note: dire means dreadful
one of the musical notes A to G

explanation.surface: A musical note within a dreadfully gloomy song.
explanation.walkthrough: This across answer is not a flower; it is one of the exceptions the preamble's 'most' allows, with an ordinary definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a mournful piece of music, originally a lament sung at a funeral.

clue.text: Square cake, if small

blocks.note: first meaning: a square number, two times two
second meaning: completes 'petit ___', a tiny fancy cake

explanation.surface: A square cake that is small, as on a bakery shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' is French petit, so the cake is a petit four, served with coffee.
explanation.definitionFit: Four is the square of two, and a petit four is a bite-sized iced cake or biscuit.

clue.text: Majority were Eton and _____ ?

blocks.note: the rest is the remainder, the larger part
the school traditionally paired with Eton

explanation.surface: A remark that most of some elite went to Eton and another famous school.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton and Harrow are England's best-known private boarding schools and historic rivals. Restharrow is a pink-flowered wild legume whose tough roots stopped the harrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Restharrow is a sticky pink-flowered plant of the pea family, found wild in rough grassland.

clue.text: Pig's Snout within - put within

indicators.note: within means inside, so one piece sits in the other

blocks.note: a sow is a female pig
Snout the tinker plays the Wall in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: Something tucked inside a pig's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S on Snout gives it away as a name, not a pig's nose: Snout is the mechanical who plays the Wall in the play scene of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow is to take something down inside the body through the throat, so to put it within.

clue.text: Archbishop Pole away from the garden with diamonds

indicators.note: things taken away from something are removed from it

blocks.note: the London street that is the centre of the diamond trade
N is north, one of the poles

explanation.surface: A churchman named Pole banished from a garden of jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: Hatton Garden is London's jewellery quarter; take away the Pole and the word garden itself. Archbishop Hatto of Mainz is the legendary prelate eaten by mice in his tower.
explanation.definitionFit: Hatto was a medieval Archbishop of Mainz, famous from the legend of the Mouse Tower on the Rhine.

clue.text: Brook, the fixer, about to turn left

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it

blocks.note: a rivet is a metal fastener
as in a U-turn
standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone named Brook, a fixer, about to turn left.
explanation.walkthrough: Brook reads as a person's name and 'the fixer' as a description of them; Brook is really the definition and the fixer is a fastener.
explanation.definitionFit: A brook is a small stream, and a rivulet is likewise a very small stream of water.

clue.text: Checkout in religious house

indicators.note: something put in a building is enclosed by it

blocks.note: a friary is a house of friars
a till is the cash register at a checkout

explanation.surface: A shop counter set up in a monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: The fritillary, or snake's head, is a wild flower with chequered purple bells; it also names a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: The snake's head fritillary is a meadow wild flower with nodding chequered bells, so fits the theme.

clue.text: Chap getting first prize for cattle feed

blocks.note: a chap is a man
the gold medal goes to the winner

explanation.surface: A farmer wins top prize at the agricultural show for his fodder.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a farmer winning at a country show, which is just where this root would be exhibited.
explanation.definitionFit: The mangold, or mangel-wurzel, is a large beet grown as winter fodder for livestock.

clue.text: Central feature of theme with 37 starting differently

blocks.note: plain reading: the core or centre of something
setter's reading: put this before 37 across, change its first letter, and a wild flower appears

explanation.walkthrough: 37 across is TEASE; HEART plus TEASE with its T changed to S gives HEARTSEASE, the wild pansy, a flower of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The heart of something is its core or most important part, the central element of it.

clue.text: Local business sound?  That's as may be

blocks.note: the hum of busy activity
a local is a pub, abbreviated PH for public house

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a local firm is sound and gets a non-committal reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning reliable, but it is the noun, a noise. A local is British slang for one's neighbourhood pub; PH marks a public house on maps.
explanation.definitionFit: Humph is a grunt expressing doubt or scepticism, like saying 'maybe, maybe not' in reply.

clue.text: Back the preacher referring to vanity

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: Rev, short for Reverend, a clergyman
vain is the adjective relating to vanity

explanation.surface: Supporting a preacher who rails against vanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as a verb meaning support, but it turns the clergyman round. Vervain is a wild verbena with small lilac flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Vervain is a wiry wild plant of the verbena family with spikes of tiny mauve flowers, valued in folk medicine.

clue.text: Shops out of Herts. town with no car

indicators.note: removing things out of something takes them away
having none of something means it is removed

blocks.note: Bishop's Stortford, a market town in Hertfordshire
taken as written
a Ford is a make of car

explanation.surface: The shops have gone from a Hertfordshire town, and so has any car.
explanation.walkthrough: Herts. is the abbreviation for Hertfordshire, the county just north of London. Bistort is a pink-spiked wild knotweed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bistort is a meadow plant of the dock family with dense pink flower spikes and twisted roots.

clue.text: Pig to be suffering with a corn

indicators.note: something suffering is battered out of shape, so the letters are mangled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the two words joined

explanation.surface: A pig in pain from a corn on its foot.
explanation.walkthrough: Pigs eat acorns, so the surface plays on 'a corn' in two ways; the letters of 'be' and 'a corn' together are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A baconer is a pig reared and fattened specifically to be cured into bacon.

clue.text: Dress, having nothing on: is setter doing the paperwork?

indicators.note: having one thing on another in a down entry places it above, so the order of parts is fixed

blocks.note: zero, shaped like the letter O
rig means to dress or kit out
the first-person form of 'is'
the setter refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: A naked setter wonders whether they are busy with admin.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts a piece above another. 'Is setter' becomes 'am I', the setter speaking for themselves. 'Paperwork' is literal: work done with paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes, so it is quite literally work with paper.

clue.text: Indicator of time on edge

blocks.note: first meaning: the verb form showing past, present or future
second meaning: nervous, keyed up

explanation.surface: A clock perched on a ledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indicator of time' suggests a clock or watch; it is the grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical tense marks when an action happens, and a tense person is anxious and strained.

clue.text: Bad film "Black Gold"

indicators.note: a bad version of something is spoilt, so these letters are knocked out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written
black gold is a nickname for crude oil

explanation.surface: A review panning a movie called Black Gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Black Gold' look like the film's title; it is a separate piece. Milfoil is another name for yarrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Milfoil, or yarrow, is a common wild plant with feathery leaves and flat white flower heads.

clue.text: Soldier's blown it

blocks.note: surface reading: a soldier has ruined his chances
setter's reading: a soldier has played the brass instrument used for military calls

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown it' is slang for having failed, but here it is literal: the instrument is blown. The same word names a blue-flowered wild plant of woods, which is the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The bugle is a simple brass horn sounding military calls, and also a creeping blue-spiked woodland flower.

clue.text: Gibbered wildly about number at the east end of the island

definitions.text: at the east end of the island

indicators.note: doing something wildly means doing it with no order, so the letters are thrown about
to be about something is to be round it

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Someone babbling about a figure at the far end of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The island' is the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast, at whose eastern tip lies this village.
explanation.definitionFit: Bembridge is a harbour village at the easternmost point of the Isle of Wight.

clue.text: Protagonist Hamlet's first off

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
a thing that is off has been taken away

blocks.note: a champion is a protagonist, one who fights for a cause
the opening letter of the prince's name

explanation.surface: The lead actor playing Hamlet has made his exit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts us in the theatre, but the protagonist is a champion of a cause. Red and white campion are common hedgerow flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Campion is a pink- or white-flowered plant of the pink family, common in hedgerows and meadows.

clue.text: Subject to time kept by bogus climber

indicators.note: a climber goes upwards, and in a down entry that runs the letters bottom to top
something kept by another is held inside it

blocks.note: sham means fake
standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone in thrall to the clock, held by a fake mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' sounds like a mountaineer or a plant, but it only tells us the letters go upward in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Maths, the British short form of mathematics, is a school subject or field of study.

clue.text: Try to sell a part

blocks.note: to hawk is to peddle goods
a bit is a part

explanation.surface: A salesman trying to sell one component.
explanation.walkthrough: Hawkbit is a yellow dandelion-like wild flower of grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawkbit is a yellow-flowered plant of the daisy family, much like a dandelion, found in meadows.

clue.text: Bowler may scatter stored grain (with health drunk in whisky?)

definitions.text: stored grain (with health drunk in whisky?)

indicators.note: to scatter things is to throw them about, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler might scatter the stumps, or here a heap of grain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' suggests cricket or a hat. The parenthesis recalls the folk drinking song 'The Barley Mow', in which healths are drunk, and whisky is distilled from barley.
explanation.definitionFit: A barley mow is a stack of harvested barley, and the title of a traditional English toasting song.

clue.text: Scots island followed by German one

blocks.note: Mull is an island of the Inner Hebrides
ein is German for one

explanation.surface: A Scottish islander with a German just behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Mullein is a tall woolly-leaved wild plant with spikes of yellow flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Great mullein is a tall biennial with felted grey leaves and a yellow flower spike, common on waste ground.

clue.text: Preliminary rounds don't start with food

indicators.note: failing to start means the opening letter is missing

blocks.note: heats are qualifying races

explanation.surface: The qualifying rounds do not begin with a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the wordplay to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is informal slang for food, as in a café sign offering 'good eats'.

clue.text: Rib, thematic if left

blocks.note: plain reading: to make fun of someone
setter's reading: add the abbreviation for left and the word becomes a wild plant of the theme

explanation.walkthrough: Add L for left and TEASE becomes TEASEL, a prickly wild plant, so the word is only thematic with an L added.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib someone is to make good-humoured fun of them, a colloquial synonym for mocking.

clue.text: Ozzie in relation to Edith Sitwell?

blocks.note: her brother, shortened to bro
pet name for Osbert, Edith's brother

explanation.surface: A question about how someone called Ozzie is related to the poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Osbert Sitwell was the poet Edith Sitwell's brother; Ozzie and Bert are both short forms of Osbert. Herb Robert is a small pink wild geranium.
explanation.definitionFit: Herb Robert is a common wild cranesbill with small pink flowers and a pungent smell.

clue.text: American invocation of Hindu belief?

blocks.note: first meaning: a US exclamation of surprise
second meaning: Hindus regard the cow as sacred

explanation.surface: An American praying to a Hindu deity.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is a playful description, not a dictionary meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is mild American slang for amazement, and the cow is a sacred animal in Hinduism.

clue.text: Thriller writer on river that rose

indicators.note: in a down entry, being on something places it above, which fixes the order

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for river
Eric Ambler, British author of spy thrillers

explanation.surface: A crime novelist writing about a river that flooded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' reads as the past tense of rise, as a river does; it is the flower. Ambler wrote classics such as The Mask of Dimitrios.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler is a climbing rose with long flexible shoots that scramble over walls and trees.

clue.text: Child makes home in endless long grass  ...

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is gone
to make one's dwelling somewhere is to settle within it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the tall tropical grass, missing its last letter
in means at home

explanation.surface: A child settles down in tall grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not the container signal here: 'home' alone gives IN, as in 'staying in', and 'makes ... in' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambino is the Italian word for a baby or young child, used informally in English.

clue.text: Charge for delivery of baby?

blocks.note: surface reading: an invoice from a midwife or hospital
setter's reading: the bird of nursery legend brings babies, and its beak carries them, while its invoice is the charge

explanation.walkthrough: Children are told the stork brings babies, so its bill can be its invoice or its beak. Storksbill is a small pink wild flower with a beak-like seed pod.
explanation.definitionFit: Storksbill, or erodium, is a low pink-flowered wild plant named for its long beaked fruit.

clue.text: ...  still in recent time equipped with this

indicators.note: something in something else is placed inside it

blocks.note: late means recent
yet means still, as in 'not yet'

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a child kitted out lately with something.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses link this to 40 down: the child is equipped with this, so the definition reaches back to that clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A layette is the full outfit of clothes, bedding and toiletries prepared for a newborn baby.

clue.text: Young beast of 38 down given lump (said Pooh)

blocks.note: surface reading: a calf of the sacred animal in 38 down
setter's reading: add 'lump' and say it as Winnie-the-Pooh does, and you get his imaginary elephant

explanation.walkthrough: 38 down is HOLY COW, so a young beast of it is a young cow. Add 'lump' and 'heifer-lump' sounds like Heffalump, the creature Pooh fears in A. A. Milne's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A heifer is a young cow that has not yet borne a calf, so the young of the 38 down animal.

clue.text: Cor! What a lot of flummery!

indicators.note: a lot of something is much of it but not all, so we take a long run of letters from within

blocks.note: the run of letters after the first

explanation.surface: An exasperated exclamation at a load of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Flummery means empty flattery or nonsense. Cor and lumme are British exclamations of surprise; lumme comes from 'Lord love me'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated British exclamations of astonishment, like 'goodness me'.

clue.text: Not so compos mentis

blocks.note: first meaning: more insane, less in one's right mind
second meaning, unstated and supplied by the theme: a wild plant with a red dye in its roots

explanation.surface: A comparison of who is less sane.
explanation.walkthrough: Compos mentis is Latin for of sound mind. The clue gives only the comparative; the preamble supplies the plant, whose root yields a red dye.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone less sane than another is crazier, and madder is the comparative of mad, meaning insane.

clue.text: Article forbidding love to American city

blocks.note: the indefinite article
grim means stern and forbidding
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
New York

explanation.surface: A newspaper article forbidding romance in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forbidding' looks like a verb meaning banning, but it is the adjective, meaning stern. Agrimony is a yellow-spiked wild flower of hedgebanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Agrimony is a hedgerow plant of the rose family with slender spikes of small yellow flowers.

clue.text: Held together without a vice

indicators.note: going without something means losing it

blocks.note: people who agreed held together in opinion
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something gripped together without a workshop clamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' reads as the clamp on a workbench that holds things together; it is the moral failing.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed, or avarice, is one of the seven deadly sins, so it is a moral failing of character.

clue.text: Young beasts with new head and feet

indicators.note: a new head replaces the old one, so the opening letter is swapped

blocks.note: lambs are young sheep

explanation.surface: Young animals given a fresh head and legs.
explanation.walkthrough: The new head is I in place of L: the two look almost alike in many fonts. 'Feet' are units of verse metre, not limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: An iamb is a metrical foot of one unstressed then one stressed syllable, so iambs are poetic feet.

clue.text: Dew on ground belonging to someone

indicators.note: something ground is crushed up, so its letters are broken and remade

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dew lying on someone's private land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a noun meaning land, but it is the past participle of grind.
explanation.definitionFit: Something owned is in a person's possession, the property of a particular person.

clue.text: Spanner for gear change

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A mechanic reaching for a wrench to fix a car's gearbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spanner' looks like the workshop tool, but it means something that spans. There is no hiding signal; the answer simply sits across the join of the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved structure bridging an opening, such as a bridge's span or a doorway's top, literally spans a gap.

clue.text: Harvester accepts a bit of luck

indicators.note: a bit of something is only a small part, here its start
to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a combine harvester
the opening two letters

explanation.surface: A farm machine gets a stroke of fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Columbine, or granny's bonnet, is a wild aquilegia with spurred blue flowers.

explanation.definitionFit: The forget-me-not is a small wild plant of the borage family with clusters of bright blue flowers.

explanation.definitionFit: Orchids are a large family of plants with complex flowers, many of which grow wild in grassland and woods.

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest a title, but the two words are separate pieces. Sedges are grass-like wetland plants.
